top_choice_rationale: P001 (Melitz and Helpman) rewards a single identifiable discovery: firm heterogeneity and selection, which made reallocation across firms a channel for gains from trade. Its originating model (Melitz 2003) is clear, and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) is a defensible second credit. It is distinct from the 2008 trade prize, which concerned representative-firm intra-industry trade and location. It is more than twenty years old and has been tested repeatedly on firm-level customs and administrative data from many countries. That tie between a framework and newly assembled micro data is what makes a claim checkable, and I weigh it heavily as an economic historian. The main costs are uncredited parallel contributors (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) and functional-form sensitivity of welfare magnitudes, so the citation should be tied to the theoretical framework. P003 (Kiyotaki-Moore) is second because its two-author credit is clean and its mechanism is mature, though its empirical identification is weaker and it sits near the 2022 prize. P002 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) has the largest policy footprint but a diffuse and contestable three-name cut from eight credited names, and it is qualified by micro evidence on state-dependent pricing. All three proposals are substantively credible, so each ranks above no award (P000).
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. No co-authorship or institutional tie to Melitz, Helpman, Kiyotaki, Moore, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. My economic history field is close to B009, which is not on the final slate.
